newsitem.title: UK: Tobacco faces fire in UK budget, drinks not so bad.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco faces fire in UK budget, drinks not so bad.

text.p: British Chancellor Gordon Brown is expected to hit the tobacco industry hard in his first budget on July 2 but give the alcohol sector a fairly easy ride, analysts said.

On tobacco, the recently-elected Labour government has adopted a tough stance on health grounds, pledging to ban advertising, including sports sponsorship, and Brown is also expected to raise duty rates.

"One assumes that the Labour party will at least continue the prior Conservative party three percent increase and it could possibly be more severe than that," said Charles Pick, analyst at Panmure Gordon.
"It's just a case of how much the industry will get penalised. All the tobacco companies are psyched up to expect a sharp blow," he added.

In the Conservatives' last budget in November 1996, then-Chancellor Kenneth Clarke raised tax on a packet of 20 cigarettes by 15 pence, by seven pence on a pack of small cigars and eight pence on a packet of pipe tobacco.

He said this was in line with a commitment to raise tobacco duty by more than the rate of inflation each year. But he said he would limit the rise on hand rolling tobacco to the rate of inflation in an effort to discourage smuggling from mainland Europe.

A 50 gram pack of rolling tobacco normally costs about 7.47 pounds ($12.22) in Britain but can be bought in Belgium for slightly under 2.0 pounds. The Tobacco Council estimate 68 percent of all hand rolling tobacco sold in Britain comes from mainland Europe and some 62 percent of that is smuggled across.
But alcohol should get off lightly in comparison in the new budget, analysts said.

"I get the impression that as with the Conservatives, Labour are fairly well disposed towards the problems created by cross-border shopping. So I think they will leave rates unchanged on beer," said Mark Puliekis, analyst at Merrill Lynch.
In recognition of the effects of cross-border shopping, former chancellor Clarke left duty rates on beer and wine unchanged for the second year running in his November 1996 budget.

At the same time, he cut the duty paid on whisky, gin and other spirits by four percent, equivalent to 26p off a bottle of Scotch. The decrease followed a reduction in Clarke's 1995 budget, the first for 100 years.

A survey from the Parliamentary Beer Club lobby group predicts that imports will double by the year 2000. It estimates that more than two million pints a day will be crossing the channel by the year 2000.

The influential drinks lobby argues that increased excise duty would mean a loss of jobs, if pubs in the south of England especially are forced to close by a flood of cheaper imports from mainland Europe. British duty on a pint of five percent alcohol by volume is 30 pence compared to four pence in France.

The lobbyists also argue that raising excise duty would result in a loss of revenue to the Exchequer by encouraging drinkers to take more so-called booze cruises to the continent where they load their cars with cheap liquor.

Clarke hit alcoholic sodas and lemonades or "alcopops," raising taxes on them by more than 40 percent or by between seven and eight pence per bottle, to help reduce their appeal to under-age drinkers.
Many health bodies dismissed that duty increase in Clarke's last budget as too low to deter under-age drinking.
The current home secretary Jack Straw launched an urgent ministerial inquiry into the consumption of alcopops in May to see what action might be needed to stop under-age drinking.

At the time of the last budget, excise duties were expected to raise 38.5 billion pounds in 1997/98 for the government's coffers. The main components are petrol and derv at 19.6 billion, tobacco at 8.4 billion and alcohol at 5.9 billion.
